newsitem.title: USA: Benthos banks on breweries - Barron's.
newsitem.headline: Benthos banks on breweries - Barron's.

text.p: Benthos Inc's new chief executive sees the company's future moving from under the sea to breweries, according to a report in Barron's.

In Sunday's edition of the financial news tabloid, Chief Executive John Coughlin said the company that made its name with high-tech underwater gear is banking on a product that can detect cracks in bottles.
Benthos, which has made equipment used to take underwater pictures of the Titantic and robots used to recover remains and debris from the TWA Flight 800 crash, has redesigned its TapTone machines.

Those devices use acoustic technology to test for small leaks in bottle. It's an item that Coughlin, who was hired last spring, believes is attractive to breweries looking to ensure their bottled beer is sealed tightly and remains fresh.
Coughlin calculates that the TapTone machines represent a potential market of $90 million. That's calculated by taking an estimated 1,500 major customers needing 3,000 machines at $30,000 each.
In fact, just last week TapTone booked nearly $1 million in new orders, Coughlin said.
He told Barron's that his long term goal is to see the North Falmouth, Mass.-based company grow sales and earnings by 20 percent a year and earn a 10 percent profit on sales.
Coughlin also did not dispute estimates that the company could earn between $1.65 and $1.75 per share in September, and between $2 and $2.20 in 1998.
